title: An honest and good heart (Luke 8:4–21)
hook: the good soil keeps the word and bears fruit with patience

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others, and your line, the women paid.

A tomato seed goes into the ground. You water it and check it the next morning. Nothing. A week later, a thin green thread. Weeks after that, maybe, something red. The waiting is the hard part. A huge crowd has gathered from town after town, and Jesus tells them a story about exactly that. "A sower went out to sow his seed." Some lands on the path, trampled and eaten by birds. Some on rock, where it sprouts and withers for lack of moisture. Some among thorns that choke it. And some on good ground, where it grows and bears a hundredfold.

Jesus explains: "The seed is the word of God." The path is people who hear, but the word is snatched away. The rock is people who receive it with joy but have no root, and fall away when testing comes. The thorns are people choked by "cares and riches and pleasures of this life." Then the good ground, with two details. In the King James words: "But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience." An honest and good heart: in Greek, kale kai agathe, a pairing some scholars say Greek writers used for a noble, upright person. And with patience: hupomone, endurance; some readers unpack it as remaining under, staying put under a weight. The good soil isn't where things happen fast. It holds on through the season. Then two short sayings. A lamp isn't lit to be put under a bed. And: "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Not just what: how. Finally, Jesus' mother and brothers arrive and can't reach him through the crowd, and he says: "My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it." Some readers take that not as pushing his family away but as widening the circle; Luke has already shown Mary keeping words in her heart. Hear and keep. Keep and do. Do, and wait.
screen: `THE SEED IS THE WORD OF GOD.`
then, large: `KEEP IT, AND BRING FORTH FRUIT WITH PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Think of something growing slowly in your life, a friendship you're rebuilding, someone else's recovery, maybe so slowly you doubt it's growing at all. Picture it as a seed in late-winter ground, where the not-seeing is part of the process; breathe in, remaining under, and breathe out the need to see results today. If you pray, you can ask for patience with slow things; if you don't, simply rest with the waiting.
Hupomone, Luke's Greek word for patience, endurance, staying under a weight: in the parable of the sower, the good soil is people who hear the word, keep it, and bear fruit with patience.
Your line: bear fruit with patience. Good soil holds on through the whole season. Day five hundred thirty-one, done.

howItsDone: The parable of the sower is often read in churches and used in Christian teaching as a way to reflect on how people hear and keep scripture over time.

original.note: Greek: patience, endurance. often explained as remaining under, staying put beneath a load.

chat.says: In the sower story, what makes the good ground good?
options: It hears the word, keeps it, and bears fruit with patience, through the season.
It's soil where the seed sprouts quickly and shows results right away.
It's soil that never faces thorns, birds or any kind of testing.
chat.meaning: Luke says the good ground is an honest and good heart that hears the word, keeps it, and brings forth fruit with patience.

hupomone.meaning: Greek for patience or endurance, remaining under

sower.meaning: someone who scatters seed by hand

kale kai agathe.meaning: Greek for honest and good, a pairing for upright people

brethren.meaning: an old word for brothers or kin

notes: kalos kai agathos (kalokagathia) as a Greek ideal of the noble person: common scholarly note. Confirm the Greek of 8:15 (en kardia kale kai agathe).
hupomone 'remaining under' (hupo + meno): standard lexicon etymology.
Day 531 is outside week boundaries; 532 is the week end.
Jesus' brothers: Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand 'brethren' as relatives or step-brothers; the script quotes the verse without comment. Keeper may want a note.
